case_name: Oberg v Saskatchewan (Board of Education of the South East Cornerstone School Division No. 209)
text:
QUEEN’S
BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation:

2020 SKQB 96

Date:
20
20 04 03

Docket:
QBG 277 of 2019

Judicial Centre:
Regina

BETWEEN:

WADE
OBERG

APPLICANT

- and -

BOARD OF EDUCATION OF THE SOUTH EAST CORNERSTONE SCHOOL DIVISION NO. 209
OF SASKATCHEWAN

RESPONDENT

Counsel:

Amanda Quayle, Q.C. and Lauren Wihak                            for
the applicant

Nicholas Cann, Q.C. and Kamara Willett                          for
the respondent

JUDGMENT
McCREARY J.

APRIL 3, 2020

I.

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The applicant, Wade Oberg, applies for judicial
review of two decisions by the respondent, Board of Education of the South East
Cornerstone School Division No. 209 of Saskatchewan [Board] by which Mr.
Oberg’s duties as
principal of
Weyburn Comprehensive High School [WCHS] were removed [Decisions]. Mr. Oberg
seeks an order quashing or setting aside the Decisions.

[
2
]

Mr. Oberg asserts that the Board
owed him a duty of procedural fairness in making the Decisions, and breached
that duty. Mr. Oberg further asserts that the Decisions are substantively
unreasonable.

[
3
]

Mr. Oberg was the principal of WCHS
in Weyburn, Saskatchewan. He spent all but two of his 27-year teaching career
with the Board. In 1997, he became vice-principal at WCHS and remained in that
position for 10 years. In 2007, he was appointed to the position of principal
at Weyburn Junior High School. In 2008, he was appointed to the position of principal
at WCHS and remained in that position until his demotion in November 2017. The
demotion is the subject of this application.

[
4
]

Mr. Oberg was demoted in
November of 2017, following an incident which occurred October 20, 2017. After
receiving reports of the incident, the Board’s administrative staff commenced
an investigation and issued an investigation report [Investigation Report]. The
Investigation Report found that Mr. Oberg had placed himself in a conflict of
interest and used his position as principal to advance his own interests as
they related to his daughter playing on a WCHS volleyball team. It further found
that this conflict led Mr. Oberg to be highly disrespectful to the community volleyball
coach and to parents and students on the day of the incident. In addition, Mr.
Oberg allowed teenaged students to be unsupervised in a pizza restaurant during
a school-sponsored trip, and allowed students to travel with parents who had
not been appropriately vetted.

[
5
]

The Investigation Report
concluded that that Mr. Oberg had: (1) used his position of authority as
principal in an inappropriate manner; (2) demonstrated significant lapses in
judgment; (3) failed to conduct himself as an appropriate role model for
students; and (4) damaged the reputation of the School Division. The
investigators determined that these failings constituted misconduct so serious
as to justify removing Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal.

[
6
]

The Board accepted the conclusions
of the Investigation Report and, on November 1, 2017, removed Mr. Oberg’s
duties as principal [First Decision]. Mr. Oberg then exercised his right to a
show cause hearing. Following that hearing, on December 5, 2017, the Board
confirmed its decision to remove Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal [Second
Decision].

[
7
]

Mr. Oberg’s application raises
the following issues:

(a)

Should the application be
dismissed for undue delay?

(b)

Did the Board breach a duty of
procedural fairness owed to Mr. Oberg?

(i)

What is the standard of review
of the Board’s decision?

(ii)

What standard of procedural
fairness did the Board owe Mr. Oberg?

(iii)

How, if at all, did the Board
breach procedural fairness?

(c)

Were the Board’s Decisions reasonable?

(d)

What is the appropriate remedy?

[
8
]

For the reasons that follow, I find
that the Board owed Mr. Oberg a high degree of procedural fairness in the
process of making the Decisions. It breached that duty in several ways,
rendering the Decisions invalid from the outset. I have also determined that
the Decisions are substantively unreasonable because the penalty imposed by the
Board does not fall within a range of reasonable alternative outcomes, even if
I accept the facts found in the Investigation Report.

[
9
]

As a result, the Decisions are
quashed. Mr. Oberg’s duties as a principal are reinstated.

II.

ANALYSIS

A.

No Undue Delay

[
10
]

On December 5, 2017, the Board
made its Second Decision to remove Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal. Mr. Oberg’s
original application for judicial review was issued on January 24, 2019, more
than 13 months later. The Board argues that this delay is unreasonable,
prejudicial and detrimental to good administration, and that the application
should be dismissed as a result.

[
11
]

I find that Mr. Oberg did not
unduly delay bringing this application. Even if there was an undue delay, it is
not likely to cause substantial hardship, prejudice or detriment to good
administration.

[
12
]

This Court has no prescribed
time limit within which an application for judicial review must be brought. However,
Rule 3-56(3) of
The Queen’s Bench Rules
provides that the court may
refuse to grant a remedy on judicial review if the applicant has delayed unduly
in bringing its application, and the delay is likely to cause substantial
hardship or prejudice, or detriment to good administration.

[
13
]

In deciding whether to dismiss
an application for undue delay, I must first determine whether the delay is
undue by considering the reasons for the delay and the explanation proffered
for it:
Henry v Saskatchewan (Workers’ Compensation Board)
(1999),
1999 CanLII 12241 (SK CA)
,
172
DLR (4
th
) 73
at para
70
(Sask CA)
. Only if the delay is undue do I
consider whether the order sought is likely to cause substantial hardship or
prejudice to the rights of any person, or whether the delay is detrimental to
good administration. Ultimately, any decision to dismiss the application is
discretionary.

[
14
]

The Board argues that Mr. Oberg was obligated to
bring this judicial review application much sooner than he did. It submits that
a specific timeline for appeal in an enabling statute is a relevant factor in
analysing whether delay is undue. Because
The
Education Act, 1995,
SS
1995, c E-0.2 sets short time lines to appeal disciplinary decisions, and
because any grievance under the relevant provincial collective agreement must
be brought within six months of the disciplinary penalty imposed, the Board
contends Mr. Oberg’s judicial review to this Court should have been brought
within a similar time frame.

[
15
]

With respect, I do not agree.
Given the complexity of the issues raised in this
application, the time it took Mr. Oberg to bring this application does not
constitute an undue delay.
The issues before this Court
on judicial review are not the same as those before the Board. The sole issue before
the Board was whether Mr. Oberg’s employment contract should be amended to
remove his duties as a principal. In contrast, the judicial review application
is multi-faceted and engages
a
complicated statutory regime under
The
Education Act, 1995

that is
rarely used and has rarely been judicially considered. The regime ousts a
principal’s right to sue for wrongful or constructive dismissal in a civil
action, which would normally afford Mr. Oberg two years to bring a claim. The
complexity of the legal and evidentiary issues raised warrants time to bring
the application properly.

[
16
]

In addition, Mr. Oberg was
required to make a request to the Board pursuant to
The
Local Authority
Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act
, SS 1990-91, c L-27.1
[
LAFOIPP
], for information relevant to this application. The documents recovered
pursuant to
LAFOIPP
took about nine months to produce. Some of those
records were used to support Mr. Oberg’s application. Mr. Oberg received the
final records he requested from the Board pursuant to
LAFOIPP
on
September 7, 2018. He filed his application on January 24, 2019. Mr. Oberg did
not unduly delay the application by filing 4.5 months after receiving the
Board’s records that were relevant to it.

[
17
]

Finally, even if I was to find
that the delay was undue, the evidence does not support that any person will likely
suffer substantial hardship or prejudice, or that there will be a detriment to
good administration, if this application proceeds. The Board permanently filled
Mr. Oberg’s position in March of 2018, less than four months after his
demotion. While undoubtedly there were legitimate reasons for the Board to make
a permanent appointment, it does not lie with the Board to rely on the fact
that it did so to create its own evidence of hardship or prejudice. Whatever
prejudice the Board faces now as a result of the terms upon which it engaged Mr.
Oberg’s replacement is a product of that engagement, not of the timing of this
application. There is no evidence that the Board relied on the fact that Mr.
Oberg had not filed a judicial review application within the first four months after
his demotion as a representation that he would not do so.

[
18
]

As a result, there was no undue
delay in bringing this application.

B.

The Board Breached Its
Duty of Procedural Fairness

i.

Standard of Review

[
19
]

No assessment of the standard of
review is required in cases where procedural fairness is at issue:
Moreau-Bérubé

v New Brunswick (Judicial Council)

2002 SCC 11
at para
74
,
[2002] 1 SCR
249
. “… [T]he assessment of whether there was a breach of procedural fairness
is not viewed through the standard of review lens. …”:
Saskatoon Cooperative
Association Limited v Saskatchewan Joint Board, Retail, Wholesale and
Department Store Union
,

2016 SKCA 94
at para
19
. Rather, the
question of whether a duty of procedural fairness has been met is a legal
question to be answered by the court:
Demitor v Westcoast Energy Inc.
(Spectra Energy Transmission)
,

2019 FCA 114
at para
26
. Quite simply,
the court must be satisfied that the process employed by the decision-maker was
fair.

[
20
]

The right to a fair decision is
absolute and cannot be remedied by the fact that a decision made unfairly may ultimately
be correct:
Newfoundland Telephone Co. v Newfoundland (Board of Commissioner
of Public Utilities)
,
1992 CanLII 84 (SCC)
,
[1992] 1 SCR 623
at  645
. Failing to use a fair
process to make a decision renders the decision
void ab

initio
¸
or invalid from the outset.

ii.

The Board Owed Mr. Oberg
a High Degree of Procedural Fairness

[
21
]

Five important factors assist in determining the
degree of procedural fairness owed by a public body to someone affected by its
decision.
The following factors are not
comprehensive, but they provide a basic framework for assessing procedural fairness:

(a)

The nature of the decision and
the process used to make it. The more the process provides for a decision
resembling judicial decision-making, the more likely it is that procedural
protections closer to the trial model will be required;

(b)

The nature of the statutory
scheme and the terms of the statute under which the body operates. Greater
procedural protections are required when no appeal procedure is provided in the
statute or when the decision will finally determine the issue;

(c)

The importance of the decision
to the individual affected. The greater the impact on the lives of those it
affects, the more stringent the procedural protections;

(d)

The legitimate expectations for
procedural fairness of the person challenging the decision, which is often
informed by any policy the public body has in place respecting processes for
decision-making; and

(e)

The choices of procedure made by
the body itself, particularly when the statute gives the decision-maker the
ability to choose its own procedures, or when the body has expertise in
determining what procedures are appropriate.

See
: Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration),
1999 CanLII 699 (SCC)
,
[1999]
2 SCR 817
at paras
23-27
[
Baker
]
.

[
22
]

A “high standard of justice is
required when the right to continue in one’s profession or employment is at
stake” because discipline “can have grave and permanent consequences upon a
professional career”:
Baker

at para
25
, referencing
Kane v Board of Governors of the
University of British Columbia
,
1980 CanLII 10 (SCC)
,
[1980] 1 SCR 1105
, at 1113 [
Kane
]
.

[
23
]

While the Board concedes that it
owed Mr. Oberg some degree of procedural fairness in its decision-making
process, it argues that the content of that duty is marginal because
The

Education Act, 1995

ousts natural justice protections. The Board generally
argues that
The Education Act, 1995
overthrows the common law duty of
fairness because the Board must prioritize the good administration of schools for
the benefit of students.

[
24
]

With respect, I do not accept
this argument. The majority of the factors informing the content of procedural
fairness support that the Board owed Mr. Oberg a high degree of procedural
fairness in the process it employed in making the Decisions that affected him.

[
25
]

First,
The
Education Act,
1995

does not oust a school board’s common law duty of procedural fairness
in favour of a general duty of good administration. In
Collins v Board of
Education of the Estevan Roman Catholic Separate School Division No. 27
,
1988 CanLII 5091 (SK CA)
,
[1988] 6 WWR 97

at para
10
(CanLII) (Sask CA) [
Collins
]
, the
Court of Appeal identified that procedural fairness obligations existed in legislation
that is substantively identical to what is now
s. 215
of
The Education Act,
1995:

10        We are therefore left with s. 206(d) which
simply says that the notice shall set out the reason or reasons for
termination. When s. 206(d) and s. 211 are read together, it becomes
immediately apparent that the purpose of the reasons required by s. 206(d) is
to provide the recipient of the notice with sufficient information to enable
him to respond to the reasons at the hearing to which he is entitled under s.
211(3).
These provisions coincide with the common law requirements of
procedural fairness. The inclusion of these procedural provisions in the
statute does not, in our view, exclude the application of the principles of
natural justice in respect of any lacunae in the statute.

This court
has, in two recent judgments,
Barrett v. Northern Lights School
Division
,
1988 CanLII 207 (SK CA)
,
[1988] 3 W.W.R. 500
; 64 Sask. R. 81, and
Knight v.
Board of Education of Indian Head School Division No. 1

(1988),
1988 CanLII 5186 (SK CA)
,
66 Sask. R. 308 (C.A.)
,

found the principles of natural justice to apply to proceedings under those
portions of the Act dealing with termination of administrative officers of
school divisions. The same reasoning applies equally to the termination of
teachers and the demotion of principals and vice principals.
Sections 196
to 226 of the
Act
[
Education Act
, RSS 1978 (supp), c E-0.1 (since rep)]
set out in some detail a
procedure designed to provide teachers with procedural fairness in matters of
termination, discipline and demotion and nothing in those provisions indicates
any intention on the part of the legislators to exclude the common law
principles of natural justice where the statute is silent. Where the statute
speaks, it must of course prevail. Where it is silent the common law rules of
procedural fairness apply. This arises by necessary implication from the
provisions of ss. 196 to 226.

[Emphasis added]

[
26
]

It is therefore apparent that the
Board owes a duty of procedural fairness and natural justice throughout any
process it employs pursuant to
s. 215
of
The
Education Act, 1995
.

[
27
]

Second, the Board’s own policies, namely AP 151,
AP 432, and its internal Saskatchewan School Board Association [SSBA] investigation
manual, suggest that a high standard of procedural fairness will be employed in
coming to decisions respecting an employee’s employment contract, and during
any workplace investigation that may affect that contract. The investigation
manual expressly speaks to the principles of natural justice including: (1) the
right to know what the accusations are; (2) the right to representation; (3)
the right to respond to the allegations; and (4) the right to know the reasons
for the decision. These four principles are cornerstones of procedural
fairness. The fact that these policies have been adopted by the Board create a
legitimate expectation that they will be employed.

[
28
]

Third, the Board’s Decisions substantially affected
Mr. Oberg’s employment. It goes without saying that the Decisions had a
significant impact on his life. Such impact necessitates a high standard of
justice and fairness:
Kane

at 1113.

[
29
]

As a result, I find that the
Board owed Mr. Oberg a high degree of procedural fairness in the process it
employed to come to the Decisions.

iii.

Content of Procedural
Fairness in the Investigation

[
30
]

Much turns on the Board’s
investigation into Mr. Oberg’s conduct and, consequently, I have considered that
investigation in some detail.

[
31
]

The Board argues that there is
no prescribed content to the duty to be fair in the context of an investigation.
It contends that the content of the duty to be fair at the investigative stage
depends on the legislative regime under which the investigation is being
conducted, the nature of the complaint, and the stage of the adjudication
process at which the investigation is being conducted. The Board submits that
when the outcome of an investigation does not result in a decision, but instead
triggers the opportunity for a hearing, the standard of fairness is reduced:
Abouhamra
v Prairie North Regional Health Authority,
2016 SKQB 293
,
16 Admin LR (6
th
)
265
.

[
32
]

I do not agree that the Board
was entitled to conduct its investigation of Mr. Oberg at a reduced level of
fairness. On the contrary, I find that it was required to conduct its
investigation in good faith, employing a high degree of procedural fairness.

[
33
]

First, the Board adopted the SSBA’s
investigation manual which suggests a high level of procedural fairness will be
employed in any workplace investigation. As I have already noted, the Board’s
adoption of the investigation manual triggers a legitimate expectation that it will
be followed. The doctrine of legitimate expectations is an extension of the
rules of natural justice and procedural fairness. When a public decision-maker
has set out specific procedures for conducting its affairs, the doctrine of
legitimate expectations applies to protect a procedural
or substantive interest when a public authority fails to follow those
procedures.

[
34
]

Second, the investigation was
the only stage of the adjudication process where evidence was weighed in making
the First Decision. This suggests that the investigation needed to be highly procedurally
fair, because the Board initially relied solely on the findings of the
Investigation Report. While in some cases investigatory shortcomings may be
remedied by a subsequent hearing , which includes an opportunity to test the
evidence, such opportunity did not exist here (see, for example,
Mondesir v
Manitoba Association of Optometrists
(1998),
1998 CanLII 19440 (MB CA)
,
163 DLR (4
th
) 703
(Man CA)
). The Board did not know whether a show cause hearing would follow its
First Decision because the show cause hearing was not mandatory unless
requested by Mr. Oberg:
s. 215(3)
of
The
Education Act, 1995
. If Mr.
Oberg chose not to require a show cause hearing, then the Board’s First
Decision would be its final decision, based solely on the Investigation Report.
As a result, it was important that the investigation be highly procedurally
fair in case it was the only mechanism which ever assessed the evidence.

[
35
]

Finally, while the Board is governed
by
The
Education Act, 1995
,
it is still bound by common law rules of
natural justice and good faith dealing. A public body must exercise its
statutory powers in relation to an employee’s employment contract according to
the rules of administrative law, which dictate procedural fairness and natural
justice, even in circumstances where the employment contract may be terminated
at pleasure:
Knight v Indian Head School Division No. 19
,
1990 CanLII 138 (SCC)
,
[1990] 1 SCR
653
at 668 and 675
.

[
36
]

Conducting a fair workplace investigation
requires considering bias, thoroughness, and the employee’s right to reply and
be heard. Many Canadian courts have
criticized employers for failing to provide employees with a fair and
fulsome opportunity to respond. While an employer need not be perfect, cumulative
mistakes in an investigation can amount to a breach of procedural fairness and
constitute a failure to act in good faith.

[
37
]

Indeed, Canadian courts have
found that the following errors in workplace investigations constitute a
failure to act in good faith:

•

Failing to act
impartially:
Doyle v Zochem Inc.
,
2017 ONCA 130
[
Doyle
]
;
Karmel
v Calgary Jewish Academy
,
2015 ABQB 731
[
Karmel
]
;
Elgert v Home
Hardware Stores Ltd.
,
2011 ABCA 112
,
336 DLR (4th) 313
[
Elgert
]
;
Chapell v Canadian
Pacific Railway Company
,
2010 ABQB 441
,
29 Alta LR (5
th
) 380
[
Chapell
]
;
and
Faghihi v 2204159 Ontario Inc.
,
2016 HRTO 1109
;

•

Rushing to judgment
before obtaining the facts:
Elgert; Lalonde v Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc.
,

2017 ABQB 374
[
Lalonde
]
;

•

Failing to be
transparent or honest with the accused employee during the investigation
process:
Elgert; Karmel; Piresferreira v Ayotte
,
2010 ONCA 384
,
319 DLR
(4th) 665
;

•

Failing to provide
particulars of allegations to an accused employee:
Chapell; Elgert
;

•

Failing to provide the
accused employee with an adequate opportunity to explain or respond:
Doyle;

Elgert; Lalonde; Chapell
;

•

Failing to consider an
employee's response:
Karmel; Chapell
;

•

Failing to interview
witnesses with potentially relevant information:
Elgert; Lalonde
;

•

Failing to consider
other evidence, such as surveillance or computer records, which might be
relevant to the investigation:
Lau v Royal Bank of Canada,
2015 BCSC
1639
and
Lau v Royal Bank of Canada
,

2017 BCCA 253
,
415 DLR (4th) 166
; and

•

Failing to follow the employer's
own policies regarding the conduct of workplace investigations:
Elgert; Frolov
v Mosregion Investment Corporation
,
2010 HRTO 1789
.

[
38
]

This list of procedural failures
is not comprehensive, but it highlights some of the common failures in
investigations that breach the duty of procedural fairness. A number of these
failures exist in the Board’s investigation into Mr. Oberg’s conduct.

C.

Breaches of Procedural
Fairness

[
39
]

Mr. Oberg argues that the Board
breached the duty of procedural fairness it owed him by: (1) failing to provide
him with written notice of the complaints against him; (2) failing to provide
him with a right to respond to the Investigation Report; (3) prohibiting him
from speaking with anyone involved in the incident while not prohibiting those
involved from speaking to each other; (4) failing to provide him with the opportunity
to be heard prior to making the First Decision; (5) failing to provide him with
the specific nature of the allegations against him and the identities of the
complainants; (6) failing to provide him with the information relied on by the
investigators and the Board; (7) failing to provide adequate reasons for the
Decisions; (8) failing to follow the Board’s internal progressive discipline
policy; delegating the First Decision to the investigators; and (9) delegating
the Second Decision to the investigators and legal counsel.

[
40
]

It is not necessary for me to
deal with every breach alleged by Mr. Oberg in order to come to a decision in
this matter. I have identified three significant breaches of fairness in the
Board’s procedure, the cumulative effect of which render the Board’s Decisions
void
ab initio
.

[
41
]

I find that the Board breached
its duty to be procedurally fair in three fundamental ways, by failing to
provide Mr. Oberg with:

(a)

Sufficient particulars of the
allegations;

(b)

A fair opportunity to respond
(the
audi alteram partem
principle); and

(c)

Sufficient reasons for a
decision that affected him significantly.

(i)

Failing to Provide Particulars
and a Fair Opportunity to Be Heard

[
42
]

The first and second breaches I
have outlined are perhaps the most significant as they are the central tenets
of procedural fairness: knowing the case one has to meet and being given an
opportunity to meet it. I find that during the investigation, the investigators
failed to provide Mr. Oberg with sufficient particulars of the allegations
against him. As a result, he was not provided with a fair opportunity, meaning a
thorough and complete opportunity, to respond to those allegations during the
investigation.

[
43
]

Mr. Oberg was interviewed on
October 30, 2017, after the investigators met with seventeen other people who
had information respecting the October 20, 2017 incident. The investigators
also raised an earlier incident of September 19, 2017, where it was alleged
that Mr. Oberg behaved inappropriately in a meeting with the community
volleyball coach. The investigators advised Mr. Oberg that it was alleged he
had engaged in four types of misconduct: (1) conflict of interest; (2) inappropriate
use of authority; (3) failure to supervise students; and (4) damage to the
reputation of the School Division.

[
44
]

The evidence filed by the Board,
which consists of an affidavit from an investigator, the agenda for Mr. Oberg’s
October 30, 2017 interview, and the questions for that interview, demonstrates
that Mr. Oberg was asked open-ended questions relating to the broader
allegations of misconduct. He was asked to provide his account of what had
occurred on October 20, 2017 and on September 19, 2017.
The investigators also put specific allegations to Mr. Oberg
respecting his meeting with the community coach on September 19, 2017. This was
appropriate and procedurally fair. However, specifics needed to be provided for
each and every allegation that investigators ultimately relied upon to support
their conclusions. This was not done.

[
45
]

For example, the Investigation
Report
provides a summary of findings. I have reviewed
these findings and have identified several key incidents where findings of fact
were made and the investigators came to a determination of misconduct based on
those facts, but the facts relied upon were not expressly put to Mr. Oberg. For
example,
the investigators found that Mr.
Oberg spoke aggressively to the community coach in public, saying: “… you just
don’t get it”; “This is your last game, enjoy it”, and “Enjoy this game it will
be your last one”. They also found that
Mr. Oberg was
“visibly angry and upset” at a volleyball tournament, had yelled at the
community coach, and that she felt “bullied” by him. The investigators found that

Mr. Oberg told the coach that she would
be dismissed if his daughter was not played for the entire match. They also
found that Mr. Oberg
told a parent: “You better watch
yourself”
. There are other examples
throughout the Investigation Report, but I need not identify every one.
Finally, investigators provided quotations from a conversation between Mr.
Oberg, students and parents on October 20, 2017, stating that the conversation
was a “general summary of the meeting compiled through interview sources.” However,
there is no evidence that these findings or the “summary” of the meeting, were
put directly to Mr. Oberg for his response.

[
46
]

While I note that the Board’s evidence states
that Mr. Oberg’s responses to questions were noted, any notes taken from the
interview were not exhibited for the court’s review. To ensure that an employee’s
responses to allegations are accurately reflected and conveyed to any
decision-maker, it is an essential practice to take detailed notes in any
investigation meeting, or to record the meeting. Notes create a record that
helps to support
transparency,
justification and intelligibility. If
such notes
supported that the specific allegations relied upon to found the investigator’s
conclusions were put to Mr. Oberg, I would have expected those notes to be
exhibited as part of the record for the court’s review.

[
47
]

Significantly, the investigators concluded that Mr. Oberg had
engaged in bullying or harassment, contrary to the Board’s policies. Mr. Oberg
asserts that it was never put to him that he had harassed or bullied a student
or other person in his role as principal. Again, from my review of the record,
there is no evidence to support that this allegation was put directly to Mr.
Oberg - as it needed to be.

[
48
]

In order to ensure that an employee is given an
opportunity to be heard, it is crucial that specific findings that are relied
upon to come to a conclusion are put expressly to the employee for a response. To
ensure this practically, it is often necessary to re-interview the employee at
the conclusion of an investigation to put the investigator’s factual
conclusions to him or her to give a final opportunity to respond. Given that
the Investigation Report contained findings of fact consisting of quotations
and reconstructed conversations, this was an appropriate case to re-interview
Mr. Oberg after a draft of the Investigation Report was complete in order to give
him a fair opportunity to respond.

[
49
]

I therefore find that the investigation was not
procedurally fair because the investigators did not put all the express
allegations they relied upon to found their conclusions to Mr. Oberg. As a
result, he was not given a fair opportunity to respond.

(ii)

Failure to Provide
Reasons

[
50
]

I find that the Board’s failure
to provide reasons for the Second Decision also breached the duty of procedural
fairness it owed to Mr. Oberg.

[
51
]

Failing to provide reasons for a
decision can be a breach of procedural fairness:
Newfoundland and Labrador
Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board)
,
2011 SCC 62
at
paras
13-20
,
[2011] 3 SCR 708
. In some circumstances, the duty of procedural
fairness requires the decision-maker to provide a written explanation for its
decision, particularly where the decision has important significance for the
individual and there may be mechanisms for the individual to challenge it.
In
Baker

at para
43
,
the Supreme Court stated that “… It would be unfair for
a person subject to a decision … which is so critical to their future not to be
told why the result was reached”. Similarly, in the recent decision of
Canada
(Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov
,
2019 SCC 65
at para
95

[
Vavilov
]
, the Supreme Court confirmed that the exercise of public power
must be “justified, intelligible and transparent” to the individuals who are
affected by it. Reasons help to demonstrate transparency, intelligibility and
justification, particularly when there are conflicting versions of events.

[
52
]

Mr. Oberg asserts that the Board
provided no reasons for its Decisions, although he concedes that it could be
inferred that the Board’s reasons for its First Decision are contained in the Investigation
Report.

[
53
]

The Investigation Report was
completed and submitted to the Board on November 1, 2017. It concluded that Mr.
Oberg had engaged in professional misconduct and recommended that his duties as
principal of WCHS be revoked. The Investigation Report was provided to the Board
prior to its November 1, 2017 meeting, following which the Board made the First
Decision to remove Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal.

[
54
]

On November 6, 2017, Mr. Oberg
was given formal notice of the First Decision, dated November 3, 2017. The
First Decision set out four reasons for the demotion, and nothing else: (1) he
used his position of authority as principal in an inappropriate manner; (2) he demonstrated
significant lapses in judgment; (3) he failed to conduct himself as an
appropriate role model for students; and (4) his conduct damaged the reputation
of the School Division.

[
55
]

On November 7, 2017, the Board
provided Mr. Oberg with a copy of the Investigation Report. The Investigation
Report, which was completed prior to the First Decision, concludes that Mr.
Oberg should be demoted from his position as principal for the exact four
reasons given in the First Decision. As I previously noted, the Investigation
Report contained findings of fact.

[
56
]

It is quite clear that the Board
adopted the four central conclusions of the Investigation Report and relied on
its findings of fact. It my view, it was not unfair for the Board to adopt the Investigation
Report as its reasons for the First Decision, although it should have communicated
this clearly to Mr. Oberg. In any event, the duty of procedural fairness was
met at this step because Mr. Oberg had an opportunity, pursuant to
s. 215(3)
of

The
Education Act, 1995
, to challenge the conclusions of the Investigation
Report and the First Decision at a show cause hearing. He was provided with a
copy of the Investigation Report that contained the Board’s reasons prior to
that hearing, which provided him with sufficient reasons to prepare a
meaningful response.

[
57
]

The show cause hearing was held
December 5, 2017 at 1:30 pm. Following the hearing, the Board confirmed its
First Decision to remove Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal. This was the Second
Decision. Mr. Oberg did not receive any written correspondence respecting the
Second Decision. Instead, the Deputy Director of the school division telephoned
Mr. Oberg on behalf of the Board at approximately 6:30 pm on December 5, 2017
and simply advised him that the Board had upheld the First Decision.

[
58
]

The Minutes of the December 5,
2017 Board meeting, which were not provided by the Board to Mr. Oberg as part
of its communication of the Second Decision, record that “the Board has
considered the information provided at the show cause hearing”. The Board
decided to “uphold motion 17-78 made on November 1, 2017 to adopt the
recommendation of the Director of Education as set out in her Report to the
Board of Education”.

[
59
]

As such, it is apparent that the
Board did not provide any reasons for the Second Decision following the show
cause hearing. The Board’s failure to do so is highly problematic.

[
60
]

The purpose of the show cause
hearing was to provide Mr. Oberg with an opportunity - in this case the sole
opportunity - to address the decision-maker. This was his chance to challenge
the facts found in the Investigation Report, present his side of the story, and
make submissions respecting why the demotion was not justified. The show cause
hearing is a mechanism of procedural fairness because it provides the
respondent who is affected by a decision with an opportunity to be heard.

[
61
]

The most basic rules of
procedural fairness are that a decision-maker must: (1) provide those affected
with an opportunity to be heard; (2) listen; and (3) not make a decision until
listening to and considering the submissions of those affected. As
noted by the
Supreme Court of Canada in
Vavilov

at para
127
,
“… The concept of
responsive reasons is inherently bound up with this principle [the right to be
heard] because reasons are the primary mechanism by which decision-makers
demonstrate that they have actually
listened
to the parties.” [emphasis
in original]

[
62
]

The Second Decision is the same
as the First Decision, but the Board provided no explanation as to why it
evidently rejected Mr. Oberg’s submissions in their entirety. Given the
significant impact the Second Decision had on Mr. Oberg’s life and livelihood,
this is highly unfair. It is a breach of procedural fairness because the Board
cannot demonstrate that it listened to Mr. Oberg at the show cause hearing and
considered his submissions before making the Second Decision, as it was
required to do.

(iii)     Other
Issues of Fairness

[
63
]

Mr. Oberg submits it was also a
breach of procedural fairness to allow Ms. Carolynn Little, one of the authors
of the Investigation Report, to participate in the show cause hearing.

[
64
]

There is conflicting evidence on
this issue. Ms. Little deposes that she attended the show cause hearing but did
not participate. Mr. Oberg deposes that Ms. Little did participate in the
hearing, offering a lengthy review of the Investigation Report, as well as rebutting
Mr. Oberg’s submissions.

[
65
]

I cannot resolve these
conflicting affidavits on the other evidence before me. Ultimately, my decision
in this case need not turn on this issue because I have already determined that
other breaches of procedural fairness are fatal to the Board’s Decisions. However,
if Ms. Little did participate in the show cause hearing and make submissions to
rebut Mr. Oberg’s case, this was procedurally unfair.

[
66
]

Section 215(3)
of
The

Education Act, 1995

places the onus on the teacher/principal to show cause
why his or her contract of employment should not be amended. The fact that the
onus is on the employee to convince the employer distinguishes this situation
from other disciplinary hearings where the onus rests with the decision-maker
to show cause. Under the process dictated by
s. 215
of
The Education Act,
1995,
the Board was entitled to make the First Decision without hearing
submissions from Mr. Oberg, relying solely on the findings of the Investigation
Report. Its decision stood unless Mr. Oberg could disprove it. In these
circumstances, a fair process required that Mr. Oberg’s submissions at the show
cause hearing be heard without rebuttal.

(iv)      Conclusion
Regarding Breaches of Procedural Fairness

[
67
]

In conclusion, the cumulative
effect of the deficiencies I have found in the processes used by the Board to
make its Decisions render the Decisions unsustainable. The Decisions are
void
ab initio
or invalid from the outset.

D.

The Decisions Are
Unreasonable

[
68
]

Aside from the issue of whether
the Decisions were made through a procedurally fair process, I have also considered
whether the Decisions are substantively reasonable in the circumstances of this
case.
Reasonableness is the standard of review of the
penalty imposed by the Board on Mr. Oberg through the Decisions:
Vavilov

at paras
16 and 25
;
Dunsmuir v New Brunswick
,
2008 SCC 9

at para

47
,
[2008] 1 SCR 190
[
Dunsmuir
]
.
A decision is unreasonable when,
among other things, it does not fall within a range of reasonable alternatives,
defensible in light of the facts and the law.

[
69
]

As I noted, I have determined
that the procedure employed by the Board to arrive at its Decisions was unfair.
The unfairness in the procedure calls into question whether the facts found in
the investigation are accurate, and whether the Board considered all the relevant
evidence prior to making its Decision. However, even if I accept that the facts
found in the Investigation Report are accurate, I find that the disciplinary
penalty imposed by the Board was unreasonable, in light of the Board’s enabling
statute, its own administrative policies, and the relevant factual and legal
limitations that establish the reasonable alternative outcomes in a situation
such as this.

[
70
]

In
Vavilov
,
the Supreme
Court considered the two types of fundamental flaws that render a decision
unreasonable. The first is a failure of rationality internal to the reasoning
process. The second, relevant to this case, is when a decision is untenable in
light of the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on it. Elements
that inform whether the decision is reasonable include, but are not limited to,
the governing statutory scheme, other relevant statutory or common law,
principles of statutory interpretation, the evidence before the decision-maker,
the submissions of the parties, the past practices and decisions of the
administrative body, and the potential impact of the decision on the individual
to whom it applies:
Vavilov
at para
106
.

[
71
]

In this case,
The
Education
Act, 1995

replaces the common law jurisdiction over wrongful or
constructive dismissal of teachers and administrators in Saskatchewan. However,
this does not mean that common law principles are not relevant to the question
of whether the penalty imposed for misconduct was reasonable. All employers are
required to consider proportionality in determining the appropriate penalty for
misconduct, having regard to all the surrounding circumstances, including the
mitigating circumstances. This was clearly articulated by the Supreme Court of
Canada in
McKinley v BC Tel
,

2001 SCC 38
at para
53
,
[2001] 2 SCR
161
, and is worth repeating:

[53] Underlying the approach I propose is
the principle of proportionality. An effective balance must be struck between
the severity
of
an employee’s misconduct
and the sanction imposed. The importance
of
this
balance is better understood by considering the sense
of
identity
and self-worth individuals frequently derive from their employment, a concept
that was explored
in
Reference Re Public
Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.)
,
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 313
, where Dickson C.J. (writing in
dissent) stated at p. 368:

Work is one
of
the most fundamental aspects in a person's life,
providing the individual with a means
of
financial
support and, as importantly, a contributory role in society. A person's
employment is an essential component
of
his
or her sense
of
identity, self‑worth
and emotional well‑being.

…

[
72
]

Mr. Oberg’s workplace was governed
by a 10-step performance management policy, AP 432. While I agree with the
Board that this policy was aimed at performance management, rather than
misconduct, it is undisputed that teachers and administrators in this workplace
are subject to progressive discipline. Progressive discipline is founded, in
part, on proportionality. While a progressive discipline policy does not mean
that an employee can never be justly dismissed or demoted without first
imposing less serious discipline, it does mean that if a severe penalty is the
first penalty imposed, then the misconduct at issue must be proportionate to
that penalty.

[
73
]

A reasonable decision is one
that is justifiable on the facts and the law: “… The decision maker must take
the evidentiary record and the general factual matrix that bears on its
decision into account, and its decision must be reasonable in light of them …”:

Vavilov
at para
126
. Accepting the facts found in the Investigation
Report, Mr. Oberg engaged in misconduct. He placed himself in a conflict of
interest and then used his position as principal to advance his own interests
(as they related to his daughter playing high school volleyball). He was highly
disrespectful to a community coach and to parents and students. Finally, he
allowed teenaged students to be unsupervised in a pizza restaurant during a
school-sponsored trip, and allowed students to travel with parents who had not
been appropriately vetted.

[
74
]

This behaviour constitutes
professional misconduct deserving of discipline. However, the penalty imposed by
the Board does not fall within the range of reasonable outcomes for misconduct
of this type, given the facts found by the Board’s investigation, the significant
and uncontroverted mitigating factors, and legal authority concerning this type
of misconduct.

[
75
]

The uncontroverted mitigating factors
are:

(a)

Mr. Oberg’s length of service is
significant. He was employed by the Board for 25 years, and employed as an
administrator (either vice-principal or principal) for 20 years prior to his
demotion;

(b)

Mr. Oberg has no prior
disciplinary record;

(c)

The misconduct consisted of a
single incident, with some additional evidence of conflict with the community
coach for a short period prior to the single incident. There was no pattern of
inappropriate behaviour or evidence of a failure to correct inappropriate
behaviour; and,

(d)

Mr. Oberg expressed remorse for his
behaviour and acknowledged that he made a mistake.

[
76
]

The absence of reasons for the
Board’s Second Decision makes it difficult to determine what weight, if any,
the Board placed on the mitigating factors I have outlined. As
noted by Chief
Justice Wagner in
Vavilov
at para
138
, “… it is perhaps inevitable that
without reasons, the analysis will then focus on the outcome rather than on the
decision maker’s reasoning process…” In the absence of reasons, I have
considered the whole of the record and the context in which the Decisions were
taken to determine whether the Board’s Decisions fell within a range of
reasonable outcomes. I find that they do not. Given that Mr. Oberg has no prior
disciplinary history, ending his long career as an educational administrator on
the basis of a single incident of misconduct, albeit one that is embarrassing,
humiliating and regrettable, but nevertheless did not strike at the heart of
his employment, is a disproportionate response. It does not fall within the
range of reasonable alternatives demonstrated in the existing law.

[
77
]

In the circumstances of this
case, demotion is as serious a penalty as dismissal. Demotion represents
a significant variation to the employee's
contract of employment. While
The
Education Act, 1995

contemplates that
Mr. Oberg’s contract could be amended to remove his principal duties with
notice, just cause is required to remove those duties without notice. In Mr.
Oberg’s case, removing his duties as a principal when he had worked as an
administrator for 20 of his 25 years of employment with the Board constitutes a
fundamental or substantial change to his contract of employment, which is akin
to a dismissal:
Farber v Royal Trust Co.
,
1997 CanLII 387 (SCC)
,
[
1997] 1 SCR 846
at para
33
;
Potter v New Brunswick Legal Aid Services Commission
,
2015 SCC 10
at para
54
,
[2015] 1 SCR 500
.

[
78
]

As I have
noted, reasonableness must be assessed bearing in mind the
context
of the particular type of decision-making involved:
Catalyst
Paper Corp. v North Cowichan (District)
,
2012
SCC 2
,
at para
18
,
[2012] 1 SCR 5
. As the Supreme
Court said in
Canada
(Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa
,
2009
SCC
12

at para
59
,
[2009] 1 SCR 339
,
reasonableness “takes its colour from the
context
”. Context includes the existing law and/or arbitral
jurisprudence
:
Dunsmuir
at para
74
;
University of
Saskatchewan v Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local
1975
,
2014
SKQB 190
,
at para
28
,
[2015] 4 WWR 813
.

[
79
]

A review of relevant Canadian
legal authorities shows that other decision-makers have not imposed such a
significant penalty for this type of misconduct: see
Lanigan v Eastern
School Division
,

2014 PECA 3
;
Western School Division No. 47 and
Western Teachers’ Association No. 47
(2002), 71 CLAS 102;
Re New
Brunswick and Holton
(1986), 3 CLAS 26;
Saikaley v Oxford House First
Nation Board of Education, Inc.,
2015 MBQB 162
,
321 Man R (2d) 137
;
Stenson v Board of Education of Horizon School Division No. 205,
2013
SKQB 364
;
Casavant v Saskatchewan Teachers’ Federation
,
2005 SKCA 52
,

[2005] 6 WWR 31
;
Nova Scotia
Teaches Union v Pictou District School Board
(1997), 47 CLAS 103;
Collins;
Re Commissioner of the Northwest Territories v Northwest Territories Teachers’
Association
(1987), 5 CLAS 32;
Re Fearon

(1980),

32 NBR (2d) 336
.
On the contrary, the cases demonstrate that when a demotion
of an educational administrator is based on a single incident of misconduct,
that misconduct constitutes a fundamental breach of the employment contract -
going to the heart of the employment relationship. Such misconduct is far more serious
than the misconduct Mr. Oberg exhibited. I also note that when the Saskatchewan
Professional Teachers Regulatory Board investigated these same allegations,
albeit with a different mandate than the Board, it concluded that a
significantly less serious penalty was the appropriate disciplinary response to
Mr. Oberg’s misconduct.

[
80
]

In summary, the penalty imposed
on Mr. Oberg by the Board does not fall within the range of reasonable alternative
outcomes in light of the facts found by the Board’s own investigation, the
relevant mitigating factors, the principle of proportionality, and legal
authorities dealing with demotions of educational administrators for
professional misconduct.

[
81
]

As a result, the Decisions are
quashed as unreasonable.

E.

Remedy

[
82
]

Generally when a court
determines that a decision of an administrative decision-maker should be
quashed on substantive grounds, or because of breaches of procedural fairness,
the decision is remitted back to the decision-maker for reconsideration. However,
reconsideration by the decision-maker is not always the appropriate remedy.

[
83
]

If I had found only that the Board breached its
duty of procedural fairness in coming to its Decisions, I would remit the
matter back to the Board for reconsideration. However, I have also found that Mr.
Oberg’s demotion does not fall within a range of reasonable alternative
outcomes.

[
84
]

In
Vavilov
,
Chief Justice
Wagner summarized the general rule respecting whether a court should send a
matter back to the decision-maker as follows at para. 142:

[142]  However, while courts should, as a
general rule, respect the legislature’s intention to entrust the matter to the
administrative decision maker, there are limited scenarios in which remitting
the matter would stymie the timely and effective resolution of matters in a
manner that no legislature could have intended:
D’Errico v. Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2014 FCA 95
, at paras.
18-19
(CanLII)
. An intention that the
administrative decision maker decide the matter at first instance cannot give
rise to an endless merry-go-round of judicial reviews and subsequent
reconsiderations. Declining to remit a matter to the decision maker may be
appropriate where it becomes evident to the court, in the course of its review,
that a particular outcome is inevitable and that remitting the case would
therefore serve no useful purpose: see
Mobil Oil Canada Ltd. v.
Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board
,
1994 CanLII 114 (SCC)
,
[1994] 1 S.C.R. 202
, at
pp. 228-30
;
Renaud v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales
,
1999 CanLII 642 (SCC)
,
[1999]
3 S.C.R. 855
;
Groia v. Law Society of Upper Canada
,
2018 SCC 27
,
[2018] 1 S.C.R. 772
, at
para.
161
;
Sharif v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2018 FCA 205
,
50 C.R. (7th) 1
, at
paras.
53-54
;
Maple Lodge Farms Ltd. v. Canadian Food
Inspection Agency
,
2017 FCA 45
,
411 D.L.R. (4th) 175
, at
paras.
51-56 and 84
;
Gehl v. Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2017 ONCA 319
,

at paras.
54 and 88
(CanLII)
. Elements
like concern for delay, fairness to the parties, urgency of providing a
resolution to the dispute, the nature of the particular regulatory regime,
whether the administrative decision maker had a genuine opportunity to weigh in
on the issue in question, costs to the parties, and the efficient use of public
resources may also influence the exercise of a court’s discretion to remit a matter,
just as they may influence the exercise of its discretion to quash a decision
that is flawed: see
MiningWatch Canada v. Canada (Fisheries and Oceans)
,
2010 SCC 2
,
[2010] 1 S.C.R. 6
, at
paras.
45-51
;
Alberta Teachers
[
Alberta
(Information and Privacy Commissioner) v. Alberta Teachers' Association
,

2011 SCC 61
,
[2011] 3 SCR 654
], at para. 55.

[
85
]

Similarly, in
Retail,
Wholesale Department Store Union v Yorkton Cooperative Association
,
2017
SKCA 107
, Chief Justice Richards recognized that in some narrow circumstances
it is appropriate for a court to substitute its decision for that of the administrative
body. One circumstance is when only one solution is possible because no other
solution is reasonable:

[48]      There is no doubt that, as a general rule, a reviewing
court should not substitute its own judgment for that of an administrative
body. Normally, when a decision is quashed, the controversy in issue is sent
back to be dealt with afresh. That said, this principle is not absolute. While
a court may not substitute its decision lightly or arbitrarily for that of an
administrative body, there are narrow circumstances where this can be
appropriate. The first is when returning the case to the administrative body
would be pointless, such as when the body has been determined to be without
jurisdiction. The second is when only one solution is possible, i.e., when any
other solution would be unreasonable. See:
Giguère c Chambre des notaires du
Québec
,
2004 SCC 1
at paras
65–66
,
[2004] 1 SCR 3
;
Telus Communications Inc. and
Telecommunications Workers Union
,
2014 ABCA 199
at para
35
,
575 AR 325
[
Telus
]
;
2274659 Ontario Inc. v Canada Chrome
Corporation
,
2016 ONCA 145
at para
69
,
394 DLR (4th) 471
; and
Allman v Amacon Property Management
Services Inc.
,
2007 BCCA 302
at para
9
,
280 DLR (4th) 550
at 573
;
Gehl v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2017 ONCA 319
at para
54
,
413 DLR (4th) 1
.

[
86
]

The relevant body of case law, including the
aggregate of arbitral authority, clearly demonstrates that the penalty of
demotion imposed by the Board was not reasonable in all the circumstances, even
accepting the facts found in the Board’s investigation. As such, the only
possible solution is to reverse the demotion and reinstate Mr. Oberg’s duties
as principal. As a result, this is not an appropriate case to remit back to the
Board for reconsideration.

[
87
]

The Board chose to deal with Mr. Oberg under
s.
215(1)
of
The
Education Act, 1995
.
Pursuant to
s. 215(3)
of
The
Education Act, 1995,
the Board’s only options following the show cause
hearing were to choose not to amend Mr. Oberg’s employment contract to remove
his duties as principal, or to confirm the amendment. The Board’s statutory
mandate under this section provides no option to impose an alternative disciplinary
penalty. Even accepting the most serious characterizations of Mr. Oberg’s
misconduct, I have found that it was unreasonable for the Board to amend Mr. Oberg’s
employment contract to remove his duties as principal. As a result, remitting
this matter to the Board for reconsideration serves no useful purpose, as the
reinstatement of Mr. Oberg’s duties as principal is inevitable.

III.

Order

[
88
]

I therefore make the following order:

(a)

The Board’s process was procedurally unfair and,
as a result, the Decisions are
void ab initio;

(b)

The penalty of demotion imposed by the Board does
not fall within a range of reasonable alternative outcomes. As a result, the
Decisions are quashed as unreasonable; and,

(c)

Mr. Oberg is reinstated to principal duties. The
matter is not remitted back to the Board.

[
89
]

Mr. Oberg shall have the costs of this
application on Column 3 of the Tariff. The application was complex and Mr.
Oberg was required to gather significant evidence to build the record for the
court’s review.

[
90
]

Finally, I had the benefit of very able
submissions from all counsel involved in this case and I thank them for their
assistance.

J.

M. R.
McCREARY
